person.name: Mazen Khaled
person.headline: AI engineer
person.one_liner: I build ML systems and measure them honestly: every choice backed by a number with an interval.
about: I graduated from Zewail City (University of Science and Technology) with a BSc in Data Science and Artificial Intelligence in June 2026.
My projects share one habit: measure before deciding. I split data before tuning, report 95% intervals, check my graders against labels, and say plainly when the simple baseline wins.
I work with small open models that run on a laptop or one consumer GPU, so everything I publish can be reproduced for $0.
principles: A difference is real only if its interval excludes zero.
Trace every failure to the first stage that broke.
Often the simplest baseline wins. Say so.

projects.title: Crisis Triage
projects.logline: After a disaster, messages arrive faster than anyone can read them. A small model triages them in six languages, and knows when it isn't sure.

stat.label: right on the 38% of new-disaster tweets it sends alone

findings: After 17 minutes of fine-tuning, Laya sends 38% of tweets from new disasters on its own, and 94.9% of those are right. The other 62% go to a person.
Chat models are sure of almost everything: trusting Qwen3-4B's own "≥ 95% sure" sends 95% of tweets, but only 72% are right.
Fine-tuned on 40,737 examples from earlier disasters, Laya ties for best with a tuned e5 classifier (macro-F1 0.72) and has the lowest calibration error (0.010).

projects.title: FaceID Bench
projects.hook: Face unlock on a Mac in 4.75 ms.
projects.logline: Face ID's two jobs, rebuilt with open models: find the face, then decide if it's you. Every stage chosen by measurement.

stat.label: right person accepted at 1 false accept in 100,000

findings: Balanced pipeline (SCRFD-10G at 320 px + ResNet-50): TAR 0.9948 [0.9900, 0.9985] at FAR 1e-5, 4.75 ms median per attempt on an M4 Pro.
As accurate as the 640 px version (not a significant difference) in under half the time.
Laya, fine-tuned, ties Platt scaling on the final yes/no decision (paired +0.003 [-0.002, 0.008]), but costs 37.6 ms instead of 0.12 µs.

projects.title: Contract RAG
projects.hook: Ask a real contract, get the clause.
projects.logline: Question answering over 100 real commercial contracts with small open models: the clause with a citation, or an honest "the contract doesn't say".

stat.label: MRR from one line: dropping the contract's name from the query

findings: Plain BM25 over fixed 512-token chunks won search: recall@8 0.85, MRR 0.73, chosen from 189 setups on the dev split.
560 answers graded claim by claim: correctness 0.75 [0.64, 0.84], citation validity 0.87, abstention accuracy 0.94.
The grader was checked against labels first (κ 0.60). Fixing two grading rules cut failures from 282 to 185 without changing a single answer.

projects.title: Receipt VLM
projects.hook: Photograph a receipt. Get JSON back.
projects.logline: A 3B vision-language model fine-tuned on one consumer GPU, quantized four ways, and measured at every step.

stat.label: field F1 on 100 held-out receipts after QLoRA fine-tuning

findings: Fine-tuning is the only change that moves accuracy much: paired gain +0.396 [+0.345, +0.442].
4-bit is free: AWQ W4A16 differs from bf16 by −0.005 [−0.026, +0.013].
The runtime matters more than the bit width: 13.22 s per receipt in transformers, 1.05 s as AWQ on vLLM.

projects.title: Pipeline Agents
projects.hook: Four agents vs one. The one won.
projects.logline: Give it data and a goal, get a pandas/sklearn pipeline, with a record of every plan, check and repair.

stat.label: success: single agent vs the four-role team, eight held-out tasks

findings: Paired difference +0.38 [0.04, 0.71]: the simpler system won this comparison.
The critic was confident (1.0 on 179 of 181 calls) but agreed with labels only at κ 0.30.
6 of 6 runs passed on fresh data; the team used 8–9 times the model calls.

projects.title: Causal Uplift
projects.hook: Likely to buy ≠ changed by the email.
projects.logline: Which customers should get a marketing email? Eight methods, a randomized experiment held back untouched, and training data confounded on purpose.

stat.label: more profit per 1,000 customers with uplift targeting (95% CI $28–$312)

findings: The response model and the uplift tree each pick 852 customers and share only 76.
Causal adjustment sharply improves average-effect recovery under strong selection bias.
No individual ranking reaches a Qini interval that excludes zero, so the table is deliberately not a leaderboard.
